title: Bullet Cluster (NIRCam Image)
caption: The Bullet Cluster, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
credit: Image: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI; Science: James Jee (Yonsei University, UC Davis), Sangjun Cha (Yonsei University), Kyle Finner (Caltech/IPAC)

recognition.text: NASA Webb image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Foreground stars, cluster galaxies and distorted background galaxies overlap against black space in Webb's view of the central Bullet Cluster. A large, light blue spiral galaxy sits at the middle, with a massive galaxy cluster on either side of it.

The Bullet Cluster is two galaxy clusters that have collided. Each cluster's gravity acts as a lens, magnifying and bending light from galaxies behind it. Webb's sharp images revealed many more faint, distant galaxies than earlier observations, and a team measured thousands of them to weigh both the visible and the invisible mass. They also mapped intracluster stars, which no longer belong to individual galaxies.

The results show dark matter still lined up with the galaxies after the collision, while the clusters' gas was dragged out and left behind. That places stronger limits on whether dark matter particles interact with each other. An elongated region of mass in the left-hand cluster hints that it may have been through more than one collision.

understand.summary: Webb's Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam) used eight infrared filters. NASA shows F090W in blue, F115W in cyan, F150W in green, F200W and F277W in yellow, F356W in orange, and F410M and F444W in red.
understand.eye: Every filter here records infrared light, which the human eye cannot see, and dark matter itself gives off no light at all, so its presence is inferred from how it bends light from background galaxies.

explore: Lead author Sangjun Cha of Yonsei University said the intracluster light can reliably trace dark matter even in such a turbulent setting. Webb covered only part of the system, and at the time of the 2025 release the researchers expected wider near-infrared images from NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, then set to launch by May 2027.
sources: NASA release: NASA Webb ‘Pierces’ Bullet Cluster, Refines Its Mass
